opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think internal deployment is one of the most important and least visible parts of the picture. Most of our public evidence about AI capabilities comes from benchmarks and from externally deployed products. But the thing I'm most worried about, the thing that could make the transition really fast, is AI systems being used inside AI companies to do AI research and engineering. That's where a feedback loop could kick in, and it could happen largely out of public view.

So the first thing I'd want to track is something like: what fraction of the actual work of building the next generation of AI is being done by AI systems? Not in a vague "our engineers use Copilot" sense, but more concretely. How much code is being written by AI? How many experiments are being designed, launched, and interpreted by AI agents with minimal human oversight? If you had a hundred-person research team last year, what's the equivalent output now, and how much of the difference is due to AI? I'd love some measure of speedup, even a rough self-reported one, tracked over time.

Second, I'd want to know about autonomy and oversight. How long are agents running without a human checking in? What permissions do they have: can they access model weights, training infrastructure, the ability to launch large compute jobs? What does monitoring look like, and how often does it catch something? If companies are seeing incidents, an agent doing something it wasn't supposed to, or appearing to sandbag or game an evaluation, I'd really want to know about those, even in aggregate, anonymized form.

Third, I'd want the gap between internal and external capabilities. If the best models inside a company are substantially ahead of what's released, and those are the models doing the research, then the public and policymakers are calibrating off a stale picture. Even knowing "our best internal model is roughly X months ahead of our best public model" would be valuable.

And finally, I'd want to know about compute allocation: how much of a company's compute is going to AI agents running research versus humans running experiments versus serving customers. That's a pretty concrete, hard-to-fudge signal of how much the company itself is betting on automated R&D.

The underlying reason is that I think there's a real chance the most consequential moment happens as an internal transition — AI going from a useful tool to doing most of the work of AI development — and if we only watch products and benchmarks, we could miss it until it's already well underway. So I'd want companies reporting this regularly, ideally to someone with the ability to verify it, so we get early warning rather than finding out after the fact.

r001.rationale: The response proposes tracking AI’s share of code and research work, but does not specify internal pull requests on which AI does most of both the writing and the review.

r002.rationale: It does not interpret a pull-request writing-and-review fraction as a measure of how much companies defer to AI.

r003.rationale: The response asks how long agents run without human check-ins and discusses oversight, but does not identify ongoing human management, approval, or review as a bottleneck to AI-driven work.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because I think the internal use of AI by AI companies is maybe the single most important leading indicator of where we are on the path to really transformative capabilities. The thing I'd most want to track is basically: what fraction of the actual work of AI research and development is being done by AI systems, and how is that changing over time?

And I want to be careful here, because there's a trivial version of that question that's not very informative. Like, obviously everyone at these companies is using Copilot-style tools, and they'll tell you it's a big productivity boost. That's real, but it's not the thing I care about. What I care about is something more like: if you look at the end-to-end process of making the next model better—coming up with research ideas, designing experiments, writing the code, debugging, interpreting the results, deciding what to try next—how much of that chain can the AI do with how little human involvement?

So concretely I'd want to see things like: What's the longest task, measured in human-equivalent time, that an AI system is routinely being trusted to do autonomously inside the lab? Is it fifteen minutes of a researcher's work, or is it a day, or a week? Are there experiments being run where a human basically just set a high-level objective and the system did the whole thing? And how often does that succeed versus fall over?

A second thing I'd track is something like the ratio of compute spent on inference for internal R&D versus compute spent on training. If a company is burning a meaningful fraction of its compute budget on having models do research, that tells you they've found it worthwhile, which is a pretty strong revealed-preference signal that these systems are actually contributing rather than just being a nice demo.

And then the third category is the one I'm most worried about, honestly, which is the governance side. As these systems take on more of the work, what are the checks on what they're doing? Is there a human actually reading the code that goes into the training run, or is it being auto-merged because there's too much of it? Are the models being used to evaluate other models, to red-team, to generate training data, in ways that create loops where you'd have a hard time noticing if something went wrong? I think the uncomfortable truth is that the economic pressure is all in the direction of removing humans from the loop, because the humans are the bottleneck. So I'd want some external visibility into whether companies are maintaining the kind of oversight that they'd say they're maintaining if you asked them in a policy meeting.

I'd also say, from an external perspective, we don't currently have good ways of getting this information. A lot of it is commercially sensitive and companies have incentives to either overstate it, for hype, or understate it, if they think it'll trigger regulatory attention. So part of what I'd want is some structured, maybe confidential, reporting to governments or a third party on roughly those metrics—autonomy of tasks, fraction of R&D effort, degree of human review—so that at least someone outside the company has a picture of how fast this is moving. Because I think the transition from "AI helps with research" to "AI does most of the research" could happen quite quickly, and it would be a shame to only find out after the fact.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the fraction of R&D work done by AI and human review of code, but does not propose tracking internal pull requests that AI both mostly writes and mostly reviews.

r002.rationale: It does not interpret a pull request writing-and-review fraction as a measure of how much companies defer to AI.

r003.rationale: It says economic pressure favors removing humans from the loop because humans are the bottleneck, and specifically raises human review and approval of code as oversight checks.

astra-6.text:
I’d most want to track how much AI systems are contributing to the development of the next generation of AI systems. Are they mostly helping people write code a little faster, or are they coming up with research ideas, designing experiments, interpreting the results, and deciding what to try next?

And I’d want to distinguish between how much companies are using these systems and how much the systems are actually accelerating progress. You could have a lot of AI-written code without a huge change in the pace of research. The more consequential thing would be if a company could accomplish in a month what would otherwise have taken a year.

So I’d be especially interested in the longest research tasks they can carry out autonomously, how much human guidance they need, and where humans are still the bottleneck. That would tell us something about how close we are to a situation where improvements in AI substantially accelerate further improvements in AI.

r001.rationale: The response proposes tracking autonomous research tasks and AI’s contribution to progress, but does not mention internal pull requests or the fraction mostly written and reviewed by AI.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes AI use from actual acceleration, but does not interpret AI-written and AI-reviewed pull requests as a measure of how much companies defer to AI.

r003.rationale: It says human guidance and bottlenecks are worth tracking, but does not identify continued human management, approval, or review as the bottleneck.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d most want to track how much AI systems are contributing to the development of the next generation of AI systems. Are they mostly helping researchers write code faster, or are they coming up with experiments, interpreting the results, and deciding what to try next?

And I’d want to distinguish between tasks that look impressive and work that actually accelerates research. If an AI writes a lot of code, but humans spend just as much time checking and fixing it, that’s a very different situation from one where it lets a team make twice as much progress.

The thing I’d be especially interested in is how long these systems can work productively without human intervention, and whether that’s increasing. At some point, you could move from having an assistant for each researcher to being able to run many research projects in parallel, with humans providing relatively little oversight. That would be a pretty consequential change, both for how quickly AI capabilities advance and for how well people understand the process they’re overseeing.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI writing code and working with less human intervention, but it does not propose tracking internal pull requests or whether AI does most of both the writing and review.

r002.rationale: It does not frame any pull request fraction as a measure of how much companies defer to AI.

r003.rationale: It says human checking and fixing can erase the time saved by AI, and that projects could run in parallel with relatively little oversight, connecting human involvement to the pace of AI-driven research.
